docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The nanopub-java library is a Java-based library for nanopublications (see http://nanopub.net) based on RDF4J.

Nanopublications are a formalized and machine-readable way of communicating the smallest possible units of publishable information. See the What are Nanopublications? page for more information.

docs.title: Setup instructions
docs.text: The tool is released to Maven central as a Maven artifact and Docker image. There is also a CLI available.

docs.title: Install from Maven Central
Run as Docker Image
docs.text: An image is released on Docker Hub

docs.title: Run through the UNIX Command-Line (CLI)
docs.text:
To use this library on the command line, just run:

macOS, Linux, WSLWindows PowerShell 
curl -LsSf https://nanopublication.github.io/nanopub-java/install.sh | bash

irm https://nanopublication.github.io/nanopub-java/install.ps1 | iex

This automatically downloads the latest release as a jar file on the first run.

The jar is fetched from Maven Central.

Environment variables

Set these before running the installer to change its behaviour:

Variable Purpose NANOPUB_VERSION Install a specific version instead of the latest one NANOPUB_INSTALL_DIR Where the np launcher is placed (default: ~/.nanopub/bin) NANOPUB_JAR_DIR Where the jar file is saved (default: ~/.nanopub/lib)

docs.title: What are nanopublications?
docs.text:
Nanopublications are a formalized and machine-readable way of communicating the smallest possible units of publishable information. This could be, for example, the outcome of a scientific study or a claim made by a particular scientist.

Nanopublications are searchable, citable, and contain authorship and attribution information. The aim is to encourage individual scientific results to be released in a traceable and interoperable format. As such, nanopublications are an effective FAIR means of communicating scientific claims and results.

As can be seen in this image, a nanopublication has three basic elements:

  1. Assertion: The assertion is the main content of a nanopublication in the form of a small atomic unit of information
  2. Provenance: This part describes how the assertion above came to be. This can include the scientific methods that were used to generate the assertion, for example a reference to the kind of study that was performed and its parameters.
  3. Publication Info: This part contains metadata about the nanopublication as a whole, such as when and by whom it was created and the license terms for its reuse.

docs.title: Java Command Line Interface
docs.text: This is the documentation of the java cli of nanopub.java.

docs.title: Available Commands
docs.text:
You can get the list of commands by typing:

np help

In the following list you can see the short command first, followed by the classname implementing that command.

  • check / CheckNanopub
  • check-template / CheckTemplateCompliance
  • fill / FillTemplate
  • get / GetNanopub
  • publish / PublishNanopub
  • sign / SignNanopub
  • mktrusty / MakeTrustyNanopub
  • fix / FixTrustyNanopub
  • status / NanopubStatus
  • server / GetServerInfo
  • mkindex / MakeIndex
  • mkkeys / MakeKeys
  • html / Nanopub2Html
  • now / TimestampNow
  • op / Run
  • setting / ShowSetting
  • query / RunQuery
  • udtime / TimestampUpdater
  • strip / StripDown
  • shacl / ShaclValidator
  • rocrate / RoCrateImporter

Some commands are grouped as subcommands of the op command. You can list those by running: np op help

  • filter / Filter
  • extract / Extract
  • gml / Gml
  • fingerprint / Fingerprint
  • topic / Topic
  • reuse / Reuse
  • count / Count
  • decontext / Decontextualize
  • union / Union
  • ireuse / IndexReuse
  • exportjson / ExportJson
  • namespaces / Namespaces
  • aggregate / Aggregate
  • import / Import
  • create / Create
  • build / Build
  • tar / Tar

To get more information on the usage of a command just type it in. E.g.

np check

will output:

Usage: <main class> [options] input-nanopubs
  Options:
    -s
      Load nanopubs from given SPARQL endpoint
    -v
      Verbose
      Default: false

docs.title: Keys and Profile
docs.text:
Some commands use the keys in ~/.nanopub/. To generate the key pair use:

np mkkeys

The command sign takes a profile file in yaml format:

docs.title: profile.yaml
docs.text:
orcid_id: https://orcid.org/0009-0008-3635-347X
public_key: /Users/name/.nanopub/id_rsa.pub
private_key: /Users/name/.nanopub/id_rsa

docs.title: Checking the key against the network
docs.text:
Signing with a key that no introduction declares for your ORCID produces a nanopublication that is cryptographically valid and publishes normally, but that nobody can attribute to you: the registry has nothing tying the key to the person, so it shows up under an unapproved agent. A nanopublication cannot be edited afterwards, so the only remedy is publishing it again under a declared key and retracting the first.

sign and publish therefore ask the network about the key first, and warn:

WARNING: https://orcid.org/0000-... is introduced on the network, but by a different key than the
one about to sign. Nanopublications signed with this key cannot be attributed, and will show as
coming from an unapproved agent. Publish an introduction declaring this key, or sign with the
declared one.

An introduction counts only when it is signed by one of the keys it declares. The first introduction of a signer is signed with the key it declares; one adding a further key is signed with a key the signer already has, and restates that key alongside the new one. An introduction that anyone could have published for somebody else declares no key it is signed with, so it establishes nothing and the warning still comes.

docs.title: --strict
docs.text:
Refuse rather than warn:

np sign --strict nanopub.trig
np publish --strict signed.nanopub.trig
Command --strict Without it sign Signs nothing, and exits with an error naming the problem Warns on stderr and signs anyway publish Leaves the offending nanopublication unpublished, and carries on with the rest Warns and publishes anyway

On publish the flag is not new: it already refused nanopublications that fail verification, and it now covers the signing-key check as well.

The check reads the network, so it fails open: when the query service cannot be reached, nothing is reported and signing goes ahead. --strict does not turn an unreachable service into a refusal, on the grounds that a check which could not be made is not evidence of a problem.

docs.title: Template Compliance
docs.text:
Usage: np check-template [options] input-nanopubs
  Options:
    -t
      File with a template nanopub to use instead of retrieving it; can be
      given several times
    -v
      Verbose: also show the templates checked against

The command checks whether nanopublications are what filling in the templates they name would give. A nanopublication names its templates in its publication info, with nt:wasCreatedFromTemplate for the assertion, nt:wasCreatedFromProvenanceTemplate for the provenance, and nt:wasCreatedFromPubinfoTemplate for the publication info. The files can hold one or several nanopublications, signed or not, so the check can be made before signing and publishing.

For each nanopublication the command prints COMPLIES or DOES NOT COMPLY, followed by its findings:

  • An error is a statement of a template that is not optional and has no triples, a triple of the assertion or the provenance that belongs to no statement, a value that breaks a constraint of its placeholder, a template that cannot be retrieved or is for another graph, or a type the assertion template sets that the nanopublication lacks.
  • A warning does not keep the nanopublication from complying: a triple of the publication info that no template has a statement for, a graph that no template is named for (it is not checked), an introduced or embedded resource that the publication info does not declare, or a value under a name the nanopublication keeps for one of its own parts, such as assertion.

The exit status is 1 if a nanopublication has an error or a file cannot be read.

The templates are retrieved from the nanopublication network, at exactly the versions named. To check against a template that is not published yet, give its file with -t:

np check-template -t my-template-signed.trig my-nanopub.trig

docs.title: Filling a Template
docs.text:
Usage: np fill [options] requests
  Options:
    --profile
      Profile file for the creator IRI if neither -c nor the request gives
      one, defaults to ~/.nanopub/profile.yaml
    --request-of
      Print the request of an existing nanopub instead of filling one: its
      URI, or a file that holds it
    -c
      The IRI of the creator, typically an ORCID IRI; overrides the one of the
      request
    -o
      Output file; standard output if not given
    -t
      File with a template nanopub to use instead of retrieving it; can be
      given several times

The command makes a nanopublication from templates and the values of their placeholders, as the publishing form of Nanodash does. The nanopublication is not signed: sign and publish it with np sign and np publish.

A request has the parameters of a link to the publishing form of Nanodash. It is given as such a link or its query string, or as a JSON object with the parameters as its members, or as the name of a file that holds one of these:

np fill -o my-query.trig request.json
np fill 'https://nanodash.example.org/publish?template=https://w3id.org/np/RA...&param_name=Example'

{
  "template": "https://w3id.org/np/RAEFAt-QcFK0ZhqfvlsmS10BnzGJA0xwOICZXkO-ai87k",
  "param_query": "get-things",
  "param_title": "Get things",
  "param_description": "Returns three things.",
  "param_endpoint": "https://w3id.org/np/l/nanopub-query-1.1/repo/full",
  "param_license": "http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0",
  "param_sparql": "select * where { ?s ?p ?o } limit 3",
  "creator": "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"
}
Parameter Meaning template The template of the assertion. param_<name> The value of the placeholder of that name. A placeholder that has a value of its own in each repetition of a statement takes param_<name> for the first, param_<name>__1 for the second, and so on. An empty value keeps the default value of the template from being taken. param_<name>__lang The language tag of the value, where the placeholder leaves the language open. prtemplate, prparam_<name> The template of the provenance and the values for it. Without one, the default provenance template of the assertion template is used, or else “Attributed to myself/others”. pitemplate1, piparam1_<name> A template of the publication info and the values for it; further ones with 2, 3 and so on. The templates for the creator and the license (CC BY 4.0 unless a value is given) are used in any case, as are those the assertion template requires. supersede The nanopublication the new one is a new version of. It is linked with npx:supersedes, and the resources it introduces and its root definition are kept. override The nanopublication the new one is another definition of. It is linked with prov:wasDerivedFrom, and the resources it introduces and its root definition are kept. derive The nanopublication the new one is derived from. It is linked with prov:wasDerivedFrom; nothing is kept. target-namespace The namespace the nanopublication gets its URI in, instead of https://w3id.org/np/. creator, creator-name The creator, whom a form takes from the person logged in. Without one, the orcid_id of the profile is taken. space, namespace What ~~SPACE~~ and ~~NAMESPACE~~ stand for in the prefixes of a template, which a form takes from the page it is opened on.

The value of a placeholder is written as it would be typed into the form: an IRI in full, a name that is minted within the nanopublication or put after the prefix of the placeholder, or the text of a literal.

Unlike the form, the command reads no values from the nanopublication named by supersede, override or derive: all values have to be given. Parameters that would have the form read values from elsewhere, such as use, are refused.

To make a new version of a nanopublication, have its request printed, change it, and add the supersede parameter:

np fill --request-of https://w3id.org/np/RA... > request.json
# change values in request.json, and add:  "supersede": "https://w3id.org/np/RA..."
np fill -o new-version.trig request.json

The request is read out of the way the nanopublication matches its templates. It has the templates the nanopublication names, the values of their placeholders, and its creator, but not a link the nanopublication itself has to an earlier version. A template for statements written by hand gets only what the other templates leave, and nothing of what a fill writes by itself, such as the creation time.

A nanopublication that does not comply with its templates has no request; the command then lists what np check-template finds. Warnings are printed to standard error: those of that check, which can point to content the templates say nothing about and which is therefore not in the request, and the problems of the request if it cannot be filled as a new version as it is.

Nothing is written if something is wrong with a request. The command then lists all it found, and the exit status is 1:

CANNOT FILL: request.json
- The statement st1 of the assertion template lacks a value for 'param_title' (title of the query)
- No placeholder of the assertion template answers to 'param_titel'; its placeholders are: description, endpoint, license, query, sparql, title

The templates are retrieved from the nanopublication network, at exactly the versions named. To use a template that is not published yet, give its file with -t.

docs.title: Shacl Validation
docs.text:
Usage: java -jar nanopub.jar shacl [options]
  Options:
  * -n
      nanopub-to-be-validated
  * -s
      SHACL shape file

The command takes two files in the .trig format, the nanopublication and the SHACL specification or shape file. This shape-file corresponds to the profile in handle-based FDOs.

docs.title: Create a Nanopublication
docs.text:
Prerequisite for creating/publishing

To create and publish nanopublications, you need to first make sure you have a local keypair. To create such a keypair, run just once: 

MakeKeys.make("~/.nanopub/id", SignatureAlgorithm.RSA);


NanopubCreator npCreator = new NanopubCreator(true);
final ValueFactory vf = SimpleValueFactory.getInstance();
final IRI anne = vf.createIRI("https://example.com/anne");
npCreator.addAssertionStatement(anne, RDF.TYPE, vf.createIRI("https://schema.org/Person"));
npCreator.addProvenanceStatement(PROV.WAS_ATTRIBUTED_TO, anne);
npCreator.addPubinfoStatement(RDF.TYPE, vf.createIRI("http://purl.org/nanopub/x/ExampleNanopub"));
Nanopub np = npCreator.finalizeNanopub(true);

docs.title: Sign a Nanopublication
docs.text:
Prerequisite for signing/publishing

Before you can sign and publish you should setup your profile, check if it is properly set by running np profile in your terminal.

Nanopub signedNp = SignNanopub.signAndTransform(np, TransformContext.makeDefault());

docs.title: Publish a Nanopublication
docs.text:
Prerequisite for creating/publishing

To create and publish nanopublications, you need to first make sure you have a local keypair. To create such a keypair, run just once: 

MakeKeys.make("~/.nanopub/id", SignatureAlgorithm.RSA);

docs.title: Publish to the Test Server
docs.text: PublishNanopub.publishToTestServer(signedNp);

docs.title: Publish to the Production Server
docs.text: PublishNanopub.publish(signedNp);

docs.title: Verification of unpublished Nanopublications
docs.text:
Besides strict syntactical requirements a nanopub has to fulfill to be published there are a bunch of best practices, which should be honored. With the command line tool you can use 

np check myNanopub.trig -v

to see a list of issues. To ensure you only publish nanopubs that meet all best practices use the flag --strict when publishing:

np publish --strict myNanopub.trig -v

In the java API you can use 

NanopubVerifier verifier = new NanopubVerifier(nanopub);
verifier.verify();
verifier.getIssues();

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
The best practices that are verified are the following:

  • The creation timestamp of the nanopub is not in the future and not older than one hour.
  • The nanopub has a label.
  • The nanopub has a type.
  • The nanopub uses an assertion template and a provenance template.
  • The nanopub has a signer and the signer is also a creator of the nanopub.
  • The nanopub contains the graph uris: …Head, …assertion, …provenance, and …pubinfo.
  • The nanopub consists of below than 1200 triples and is smaller than 10MB.

docs.title: Reading a Template
docs.text:
A template is a nanopublication that describes how nanopublications of a certain kind are structured: the statements they consist of, the placeholders to be filled in, and the constraints on the values. Template reads one:

// Fetches the template nanopublication from the network:
Template template = new Template("https://w3id.org/np/RAEzjboN_ipuwsFnvhqAl9Fy7fZl34cGZ1QhJ-7cbbGGM");
// Or from a nanopublication at hand, such as a file that is not published yet:
Template template = new Template(new NanopubImpl(new File("my-template.trig")));

for (IRI statement : template.getStatementIris()) {
    IRI subject = template.getSubject(statement);
    IRI predicate = template.getPredicate(statement);
    Value object = template.getObject(statement);
    boolean optional = template.isOptionalStatement(statement);
    if (object instanceof IRI placeholder && template.isPlaceholder(placeholder)) {
        String label = template.getLabel(placeholder);
        String regex = template.getRegex(placeholder);       // null if unconstrained
        boolean isLiteral = template.isLiteralPlaceholder(placeholder);
    }
}

A grouped statement is one entry of getStatementIris(), and getStatementIris(group) lists its members. getStatementErrors() reports statements that cannot produce valid nanopublications.

Reading a template needs no network access. Only the possible values of a restricted-choice placeholder that are kept in another nanopublication (nt:possibleValuesFrom) are fetched, when getPossibleValues(placeholder) is first called. Pass a NanopubResolver to decide where nanopublications come from, or NanopubResolver.NONE to never fetch any:

Template template = new Template(nanopub, NanopubResolver.NONE);

getDescription() and getStatementDescription(statement) return the text as published. It may contain HTML and is not sanitized.

docs.title: Checking a Nanopublication against its Templates
docs.text:
A nanopublication names the templates it was made from in its publication info. TemplateComplianceChecker retrieves them and checks whether the nanopublication is what filling them in would give:

TemplateComplianceChecker checker = new TemplateComplianceChecker();
ComplianceReport report = checker.check(nanopub);
if (!report.isCompliant()) {
    for (ComplianceIssue issue : report.getErrors()) {
        System.out.println(issue.graph() + ": " + issue.message());
    }
}

An error is, for instance, a statement of a template that is not optional and has no triples, a triple of the assertion that belongs to no statement, or a value that breaks a constraint of its placeholder. report.getWarnings() has what does not keep the nanopublication from complying, such as a triple of the publication info that no template has a statement for. A checker keeps the templates it has retrieved, so use one for many nanopublications.

The classes underneath can be used on their own. TemplateMatcher assigns the triples of one graph to the statements of one template, PlaceholderMatcher checks a single value against a placeholder, and BindingContext holds the values bound:

BindingContext context = BindingContext.forNanopub(template, nanopub);
TemplateMatch match = new TemplateMatcher(template).match(nanopub.getAssertion(), context);
match.getMissingStatements();   // statements that are not optional and have no triples
match.getUnusedTriples();       // triples that belong to no statement
match.getViolations();          // values that break a constraint
Value name = context.get(placeholderIri);

docs.title: Filling a Template
docs.text:
TemplateFiller makes a nanopublication from templates and the values of their placeholders, as the publishing form of Nanodash does. A FillRequest names the templates and gives the values, each under the name of its placeholder:

FillRequest request = new FillRequest("https://w3id.org/np/RAEFAt-QcFK0ZhqfvlsmS10BnzGJA0xwOICZXkO-ai87k")
        .set("query", "get-things")
        .set("title", "Get things")
        .set("description", "Returns three things.")
        .set("endpoint", "https://w3id.org/np/l/nanopub-query-1.1/repo/full")
        .set("license", "http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0")
        .set("sparql", "select * where { ?s ?p ?o } limit 3")
        .setCreator(creatorIri);
try {
    Nanopub nanopub = new TemplateFiller().fill(request);   // not signed
} catch (TemplateFillException ex) {
    ex.getProblems().forEach(System.out::println);
}

The nanopublication gets the template links, the introduced and embedded resources, the types and the label that the form would give it. Its provenance and publication info are made from the templates the request names, and otherwise from the default provenance template of the assertion template, or “Attributed to myself/others”, and from the templates for the creator and the license.

A value is written as it would be typed into the form: an IRI in full, a name that is minted within the nanopublication, or the text of a literal. A statement that is repeated takes the values name, name__1, name__2 and so on; request.getValues().add("name", "...") gives the next one. Nothing is made if something is wrong: TemplateFillException lists all values that are missing or break a constraint, all names no placeholder answers to, and all values that would be lost because the statement they belong to is left out.

A request has the parameters of a link to the publishing form of Nanodash, and is read from and written as one with FillRequest.fromUrl, fromJson, toQueryString and toJson.

To make a new version of a nanopublication, read its request back, change it, and say what the new nanopublication is to the old one:

ComplianceReport report = new TemplateComplianceChecker().check(published);
FillRequest request = FillRequest.of(report)
        .set("title", "Get three things")
        .setSource(FillRequest.Mode.SUPERSEDE, published.getUri().stringValue());
Nanopub newVersion = new TemplateFiller().fill(request);

With SUPERSEDE and OVERRIDE the resources the old nanopublication introduces keep their IRIs and the root definition stays; with DERIVE everything is minted anew. The request that is read back does not have the link the nanopublication itself has to an earlier version. Read it only from a nanopublication that complies with its templates (report.isCompliant()), as content the templates do not account for is not in it.
